parts.problemMd:
Study** Figure 2**, a flood hydrograph showing river discharge following a period of heavy rainfall.

![Graph showing precipitation as beige bars and discharge as a blue line. Discharge peaks at 10-12 hours after storm, while precipitation ends by 10 hours.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/1-river-environments/1-1-the-water-cycle-and-drainage-basin-system/assets/001-graph-showing-precipitation-as-beige-bars-and-di.png)

Using **Figure 2**, describe the changes in river discharge shown.
parts.solutionMd:
After 1 hour of the storm, the discharge was just under 25 cumecs. **[1]** The discharge then rose quickly, reaching a peak of 200 cumecs at approximately 11 hours after rainfall began. **[1]** After the peak, discharge fell  gradually over the remaining hours, dropping to around 22 cumecs by hour 21 and returning to its base flow. **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**describe**' means that the answer needs to state what the graph shows, **using data from Figure 2** where possible. No explanation of why changes occur is required.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a** point-marked** approach.
> 
> - **One mark **for each valid descriptive point, using data from Figure 2, up to a maximum of 3 marks
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Reference to the lag time, if clearly identified from the figure
> - Description of the overall shape of the hydrograph as having a short lag time
> - Any other appropriate response
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Explaining the causes of the hydrograph shape [for example, referring to impermeable rock or urbanisation] rather than describing what the graph shows
> - Describing only one feature of the graph, such as the peak, and miss the rising limb, falling limb, and base flow
> - Failing to quote any data values from the figure; using figures from the graph is expected and gains credit

> **[exam-tip]**
> **For** 'describe the changes' questions using a graph, always work from left to right: start at the beginning, describe what happens in the middle, and finish at the end.
> 
> **Aim** for three separate observations to match the three marks available. Data equals marks; if a value appears on the graph, use it.
> 
> **Examiners** want to see that you can read a graph accurately, so quote specific numbers wherever you can.

parts.problemMd: Explain why deforestation in a drainage basin can increase the risk of flooding.
parts.solutionMd:
When trees are removed, there is less interception of rainfall, so more water reaches the ground surface directly. **[1]** Without tree roots to absorb water, the soil becomes saturated more quickly, which increases surface run-off and overland flow. **[1]** This means water enters the river much faster, causing discharge to rise rapidly and significantly increasing the risk of a flood. **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word **'explain why**' means that the answer needs to provide reasons and show understanding of cause and effect. Describing what deforestation is will not be sufficient on its own.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a **point-marked** approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for a valid point
> - **One mark** for development of a point
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Reference to the water cycle or hydrological cycle terminology such as throughflow, infiltration, and percolation
> - Reference to reduced evapotranspiration as a consequence of tree removal
> - Any other appropriate response
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Stating 'there are fewer trees to absorb water' but do not complete the chain of reasoning to explain what happens next; the explanation must be developed through to the flood risk
> - Confusing interception [trees catching rainfall on their leaves and branches] with absorption [roots taking in water from the soil]
> - Writing about the physical appearance of a deforested landscape rather than the hydrological consequences

parts.problemMd:
Study Figure 1c below

Analyse the factors that affect the river regime shown in figure 1c

![screenshot-2023-08-15-at-10-11-53](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/1-river-environments/1-1-the-water-cycle-and-drainage-basin-system/assets/005-screenshot-2023-08-15-at-10-11-53.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The river regime in Figure 1c is influenced by both the physical features and the land uses in the drainage basin. A river regime means how the discharge changes over time. At gauging station A, the hydrograph is much “flashier”, with a high peak discharge of around 70 cumecs and a short lag time **[S]**. This is because the river there flows through an urban area (shown in grey on Figure 1c), where impermeable surfaces like roads stop infiltration and increase surface run-off **[Ap]**. Water reaches the channel quickly, so discharge rises sharply after the storm.

In contrast, gauging station B shows a much lower peak discharge and a longer lag time** [S]**. This part of the basin has more forested land, shown by the tree symbols. Trees intercept rainfall and encourage infiltration, so the water travels more slowly to the river **[Ap]**. There is also pastoral farming upstream, which usually allows more infiltration than urban land, reducing run-off and slowing the response to rainfall** [S]**.

Because the drainage basin includes many tributaries flowing through different land uses, the rivers react differently to the same storm **[Ap][S]**. Overall, Figure 1c shows that human land use, like urbanisation, creates rapid changes in discharge, while natural vegetation leads to a calmer, slower river regime with a delayed peak **[Ap][S].**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word **‘analyse**’ means that the answer needs to break down the components and make evidence-based connections about causes and effects or relationships between them.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a **'level of response'** approach. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark.
> 
> The AO focus includes AO3 Analysis **[Ap]** and AO4 Skills. **[S]**
> 
> - A top-level 3 answer ** ****[8 marks]** will include specific examples that show:
> 
>   - Application of knowledge and understanding
>   - Interpretation, analysis and evaluation of geographical information/issues
>   - Judgements supported by evidence
>   - Selection of information, skills and techniques
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be included in the answer includes:
> 
> - Impact of vegetation on lag time
> - Other human interventions such as sewers, dams and water abstraction
> - Shapes of the hydrographs

parts.problemMd: Referring to a named flood event you have studied, explain the physical and human causes of the flooding.
parts.solutionMd:
During the Somerset Levels floods of 2014, several physical and human factors combined to cause widespread flooding across the region. **[1]** Prolonged and heavy rainfall over several weeks saturated the ground completely, so surface run-off increased significantly and the rivers quickly exceeded their bankfull capacity. **[1]** The flat, low-lying topography of the Somerset Levels meant that water could not drain away quickly once it had left the river channel. **[1]** Human factors also played a significant role; the drainage ditches had not been dredged for many years, which had reduced their capacity to carry water away from the land. **[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
Water quality varies across the world due to differences in pollution sources and access to water treatment, as shown in Figures 1c and 1d.

Figure 1c shows that pollution from domestic sewage, industrial waste and agricultural fertilisers reduces water quality. In many low-income countries, sewage is often untreated and released into rivers, which increases bacteria levels and makes water unsafe to drink. **[Ap]** This helps explain why Figure 1d shows that large parts of sub-Saharan Africa have over 20% of the population using untreated drinking water. **[S]**

In contrast, high-income countries generally have better water quality because they use advanced water treatment processes such as filtration, sedimentation and chlorination, shown in Figure 1c. **[Ap]**** **These processes remove harmful microorganisms and pollutants before water reaches homes. Figure 1d supports this, as Europe and North America mostly have less than 1–10% of people using untreated water. **[S]**

However, water quality can still vary within wealthier countries. Industrial waste and agricultural runoff can pollute rivers, even where treatment exists.** ****[Ap]** For example, fertilisers washed into rivers can cause eutrophication, reducing oxygen levels and harming ecosystems, which can lower overall water quality. **[Ap]**

Overall, variations in water quality are caused by differences in pollution levels and how effectively water is managed and treated. **[Ap]**** **Countries with strong infrastructure and regulation tend to have higher water quality, while countries lacking investment experience have poorer water quality, as shown clearly in both figures. **[S]**

Flood risk in Bangladesh is high due to a combination of physical factors and limited human management, as shown in Figure 1c.

One major physical factor is Bangladesh’s low-lying relief. Heavy monsoon rainfall is another key factor. Figure 1c shows widespread river and monsoon flooding, particularly in central and northern areas. **[S]**** **Prolonged rainfall saturates the soil, reducing infiltration and increasing surface runoff into rivers.** ****[Ap]**

Human factors also affect flood risk. Bangladesh has a very high population density, with many people living on floodplains near rivers, as shown around Dhaka.** ****[Ap]** Although Figure 1c shows some flood defences, these are limited and do not protect most of the country. **[S]**

Overall, flood risk in Bangladesh is high due to low elevation, heavy monsoon rainfall, snowmelt from the Himalayas and limited flood management, a combination of human and physical factors where the human factors often exacerbate the flood risk. **[Ap][S]**

parts.problemMd: Discuss the effectiveness of **two** different methods of flood control.
parts.solutionMd:
Hard engineering methods are one way of controlling flooding; these are human-built structures which aim to reduce flooding or the impacts of flooding. An example of this is the construction of dams, such as the Three Gorges Dam in China. **[S]** Dams can be used to control the amount of discharge downstream by opening or closing gates.  This means that if there is heavy rainfall, the amount of water can be held in the reservoir and released slowly into the river.**  **This can be very effective, and the Three Gorges Dam is estimated to protect about 15 million people downstream from flooding. However, it can impact on the environment and wildlife.**[Ap]**

Soft engineering methods are also used to control flooding. One method is afforestation, where trees are planted in the drainage basin. The planting of trees increases the amount of interception and infiltration. This reduces the speed at which water reaches the river, which means discharge levels do not rise rapidly, reducing the risk of flooding. **[Ap]**

Both soft and hard engineering methods can be effective in reducing the risk of flooding. **[Ap] **However, hard engineering methods tend to have a greater impact on the environment because they involve changing the structure of the channel. **[Ap]**

Hard engineering strategies such as flood walls and dams provide immediate, reliable protection against flooding. **[K]** The Thames Barrier in London has protected the city from tidal surges since it was completed in 1982, which shows that hard engineering can be highly effective in urban areas. **[K]** However, these schemes are very expensive to build and maintain; flood walls in particular need constant upkeep. If they fail, the consequences can be severe, especially if communities behind them have no other protection. **[U] **Hard engineering can also move flood risk downstream, rather than solving it at a wider catchment scale.

Soft engineering strategies such as afforestation and floodplain restoration work with natural processes rather than against them. **[K]** In Pickering, North Yorkshire, natural flood management schemes, including tree planting and leaky dams, successfully reduced peak discharge and protected the town from flooding. **[K]** These approaches are cheaper and more sustainable, though they may not provide sufficient protection during extreme flood events. **[U]**

Overall, neither method works better than the other; the best strategy depends on the situation. **[Ap]** In dense urban areas, hard engineering is often necessary because the cost of flooding to people and property is very high. **[Ap]** In rural areas, soft engineering is often more appropriate because it is affordable and sustainable over time. **[Ap]** A combined approach is arguably the most effective solution because it addresses both immediate flood risk and long-term sustainability. **[Ap]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**analyse**' means that the answer needs to examine the statement, identify key factors, consider how they relate to each other, and assess the degree to which the evidence supports or challenges the statement. Simply describing hard and soft engineering strategies will not be sufficient to reach the higher levels.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a level of response approach. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark.
> 
> AO weighting for this question:
> 
> - AO1 [2 marks], AO2 [4 marks], AO3 [2 marks]
> 
> A top-level Level 3** ****[7–8 marks]**** **answer will**:**
> 
> - **AO1 ****[K]**: show knowledge of both hard and soft engineering strategies
> - **AO2** **[U]**: show understanding of effectiveness, strength and limitation of each strategy, showing a balanced and two-sided response
> - **AO3 ****[Ap]**: apply evaluation and a reasoned judgement
> - Use accurate geographical terminology consistently throughout
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question, as it will depend on the examples used. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Reference to other hard engineering examples: Boscastle post-2004 flood defence scheme; channel management schemes in Bangladesh; levée systems along the Mississippi River
> - Other examples of soft engineering include restoring floodplain wetland areas and making sure that urban drainage systems last for a long time. Management of the retreat of agricultural land [SuDS]
> - Discussion on how cost-effective a strategy is in developing countries compared to developed countries
> - A comparison of the long-term effects of hard engineering and soft engineering on the environment
> - Any other appropriate response
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Writing about the causes and effects of flooding instead of how to manage it
> - Talking about hard engineering and soft engineering in two separate paragraphs, without linking, comparing, or rating the two methods against each other
> - Stating a conclusion but not linking it back to the original statement
> - Not using named examples, which limits the response to Level 2 at most
> - Using the word 'effective' without defining or discussing its meaning in terms of cost, reliability, sustainability, lives protected, or environmental impact

> **[exam-tip]**
> '**Analyse**' means you must go beyond description at every stage of your answer. After every point you make, ask yourself, 'So what?' What does this tell us about whether hard engineering is more effective than soft engineering?

parts.problemMd: Assess the relative importance of marine erosion and sub-aerial processes in the formation of coastal landforms.
parts.solutionMd:
The shape of coastal land is determined by how marine erosion and sub-aerial processes work together.** [AO3] **Marine erosion is usually easier to see because it removes material directly from the shore. **[AO2] **But sub-aerial processes are also important for weakening structures and making it easier for the coast to retreat from the land on a large scale. **[AO2]**

Marine erosion involves waves directly attacking the base of cliffs using hydraulic action, abrasion, and attrition.** [AO2]** This action creates the initial weakness, like a wave-cut notch, at the base of cliffs.** [AO2]** Marine erosion is responsible for wave-cut platforms, caves, arches, stacks, and stumps.** [AO3]**

Sub-aerial processes above the high tide line include freeze-thaw, salt crystal growth (physical weathering), and chemical weathering (carbonation), plus mass movement (rockfalls, slumps).** [AO2]** These actions weaken the rock above the wave-cut notch, making it unstable and causing it to collapse.** [AO3]** As a result, rockfalls widen cracks into caves, help arches collapse into stacks, and create scree slopes at cliff bases.** [AO2]**

Together they form a cycle where marine erosion attacks the bottom, sub-aerial processes attack the top, and the cliff retreats, leaving a platform.** [AO3]**

With the formation of cliffs, marine erosion forms the notch,** [AO2]** but sub-aerial processes (weathering/mass movement) cause the actual collapse that retreats the cliff.** [AO3]** On the other hand, waves exploit weaknesses that are often created by weathering to form caves;** [AO2] **marine action attacks both sides of a headland;** [AO2] **and weathering weakens arches until they collapse into stacks.** [AO2]**

Overall, although the two processes work together,** [AO2] **marine erosion is the most important because it provides the initial energy and creates the space (notches or cavities) needed to shape the coastline.** [AO3]** Sub-aerial processes mainly assist by weakening rock, but without wave erosion, most coastal landforms would not form. ** [AO2] [AO3]**

>

>

> - AO3: Apply understanding to assess the relative importance of each process, make connections, and reach a supported judgement.
>

> 
> - Understanding of marine erosion and sub-aerial processes and the landforms they create.
> - Application of understanding to make connections between processes and landforms.

Analyse the reasons soft engineering may lead to conflict between different users of the coast.
parts.solutionMd:
The term 'soft engineering' means working with nature rather than against it to reduce the impacts of erosion. **[KU] **However, not everyone agrees with this approach, and that leads to conflict between stakeholders, such as conservationists, residents, business owners, and governments. **[Ap]**

The high tide line has shifted 100 metres inland since 1902, bringing buildings valued at US\$23 billion within 50 metres of the current coastline's retreat. **[KU]** It cost US\$16 billion to build a dune ecosystem, but the land is still being eroded. **[Ap]** In 2018, the local government agreed to allow a sea wall breach to enable the coast to move naturally,  **[KU] **despite valuable land, including a golf course and major roads, being in the path of the projected 2050 high tide. **[Ap]**

Different stakeholders want different things. **[Ap] **Local residents and business owners are likely to be angry about the 'managed retreat'. **[Ap] **They see US\$18 billion worth of property at risk. **[KU] **They usually want 'hard engineering' (like sea walls) to provide a solid guarantee that their homes won't be flooded. **[KU] **They may feel the government is 'giving up' on them by choosing cheaper soft options like sand dunes. **[Ap]**

Conservationists and bird watchers like soft engineering. **[KU] **They want to see sand dunes and saltmarshes because they protect ecosystems and attract wildlife. **[KU]** However, a local business—like the golf course shown in the figure—will see the project as a disaster. **[Ap] **They are losing their land to the sea, which means a loss of income and jobs. **[Ap]**

Tourists come for the beautiful beaches. **[KU] **If soft engineering, like 'managed retreat', leads to the removal of traditional beaches or prevents access to the shore to protect delicate dunes, tourists might stop coming. **[Ap] **This can hit the local economy hard. **[KU] **On the other hand, some tourists might prefer the 'natural' look of dunes to 'ugly' concrete walls. **[Ap]**

While the government wants a sustainable, lower-cost option that works with nature, **[KU] **the immediate economic loss of US\$18 billion in buildings makes soft engineering a challenging 'sell' to the people who actually live there. **[Ap] **The coast's continued retreat despite a US\$16 billion investment in dunes **[KU] **suggests that soft engineering might be failing to provide the security homeowners demand, leading to even more tension. **[Ap]**

parts.problemMd: Assess how geology affects the formation of headlands and bays.
parts.solutionMd:
Geology affects the rate of coastal erosion because different rock types have different levels of resistance.** [A]** Softer rocks such as clay or sand are less resistant to erosion and are worn away more quickly by processes such as hydraulic action and abrasion. **[A]** Therefore, erosion occurs unevenly along coastlines, particularly where hard (resistant) and soft (less resistant) rock bands run at right angles to the sea (discordant coastline). **[Ap]**

Softer rocks such as clay or sand erode more quickly when attacked by hydraulic action and abrasion. **[A]** Over time, this rapid erosion creates bays, where the coastline is worn back more quickly. **[Ap]**

Harder rocks such as limestone or granite are more resistant to erosion. **[A] **These rocks erode more slowly, even when exposed to powerful waves **[Ap]**. This reduces the rate of coastline retreat and causes them to jut out into the sea as headlands. **[Ap]**

Wave refraction then increases erosion at headlands by focusing wave energy onto them, while bays become more sheltered and experience deposition. **[A]** This further highlights the contrast between headlands and bays over time. **[Ap]**

Geology also affects erosion through the presence of joints and faults. **[A] **Rocks with many cracks allow water and air to enter, increasing erosion and weathering.  **[A]** This makes erosion more effective and can speed up cliff collapse. **[Ap] **Overall, geology plays a key role in controlling how quickly different parts of the coastline erode.

parts.problemMd: Assess the importance of coastal ecosystems in protecting coastlines from erosion.
parts.solutionMd:
Coastal ecosystems are important in protecting coastlines from erosion because they reduce wave energy before it reaches the shore.** [Ap] **Coral reefs act as offshore barriers, causing waves to break in deeper water rather than directly at the coastline.** [Ap] ** This reduces the power of waves reaching cliffs and beaches, lowering erosion rates.** [E] **

Mangroves and salt marshes also play a key role in erosion protection.** [Ap] ** Mangroves have dense root systems that increase friction and slow down waves and tidal currents.** [Ap] **This reduces the energy available to erode the coastline.** [E] ** Salt marsh vegetation has a similar effect, lowering wave speed and encouraging deposition of fine sediment.** [Ap] ** This helps stabilise the coastline and prevent material from being washed away.** [E] **

However, coastal ecosystems do not provide equal protection everywhere.** [E] ** Salt marshes only form in low-energy, sheltered environments such as estuaries, meaning they cannot protect exposed coastlines.** [Ap] ** Coral reefs are limited to warm, shallow tropical waters and can be damaged by pollution and climate change, reducing their effectiveness.** [Ap] **

Overall, coastal ecosystems are very important in protecting coastlines from erosion where conditions allow them to develop.** [E] ** However, their importance is limited by location and environmental health, meaning they are most effective as part of a wider coastal management strategy.** [E] **

parts.problemMd: Assess the relative importance of marine erosion and sub-aerial processes in shaping coastal landforms.
parts.solutionMd:
Marine erosion is very important in shaping coastal landforms because it directly removes rock from the coastline.** [E]** Processes such as hydraulic action and abrasion erode the base of cliffs, forming features such as wave-cut notches, caves and arches.** [Ap]** Continued erosion weakens rock structures and leads to collapse** [E]**, creating stacks and wave-cut platforms.** [Ap]**

Sub-aerial processes also play an important role.** [E]** Weathering breaks down rock at the top of cliffs, while mass movement causes weakened material to fall due to gravity.** [Ap]** This increases the rate of cliff retreat, especially after heavy rainfall.** [E]**

However, sub-aerial processes usually work alongside marine erosion rather than acting alone.** [E] **Without wave erosion undercutting the cliff base, weathered material would not collapse as easily.** [Ap]**

Overall, marine erosion is the most important process because it provides the energy needed to shape most coastal landforms.** [E] **Sub-aerial processes increase the rate of change but are secondary to wave action.** [E]**

parts.problemMd: Explain **two **ways coastal ecosystems reduce erosion.
parts.solutionMd:
Coastal ecosystems reduce erosion by reducing wave energy before it reaches the coastline.  **[1]** Coral reefs form offshore barriers that cause waves to break early, meaning the waves that reach the shore have much less power to erode cliffs and beaches. **[1]**

Another way ecosystems reduce erosion is by trapping and stabilising sediments. **[1]** Mangroves and salt marshes have dense vegetation and root systems that hold sediment in place and reduce the movement of material along the coast. **[1]** This helps build up land levels and prevents sediment from being washed away by waves.

parts.problemMd: Discuss the conflicting views that affect the choice of management for **one **named stretch of coastline.
parts.solutionMd:
On the east coast of England, the Holderness coast is the fastest eroding coastline in Europe at an average rate of 1.8 metres a year. ** [AO3]  **There are several reasons for this erosion, including softrock geology of boulder clay, strong waves, naturally narrow beaches, and existing coastal defences. ** [AO3] **

The current management strategies include hard engineering, such as sea walls, rock armour, groynes, and beach widening. ** [AO3] **

Major towns like Bridlington and Hornsea in the north receive the majority of the coastline protection  via sea walls and groynes. ** [AO3] **However, these systems prevent natural sediment movement down the coast and deprive southerly towns and villages, such as Withernsea and Easington, of sand, which increases coastal erosion in those areas. ** [AO4] **For instance, erosion has increased at Great Cowden because of the groynes used in Mappleton, which have depleted sediment deposits on the beach.** [AO4] ** This has led to farms being lost through the erosion and 100 chalets at the Golden Sands Holiday Park falling into the North Sea. ** [AO4] **

Management at Withernsea has used groynes to widen the beach and also a seawall to protect the town from coastal flooding. ** [AO3]  **These measures will hold the line and calm the concerns of local residents, retailers and visitors to the beach. ** [AO3]  **However, costs have limited the size of the sea wall and increased wave noise. The rock armour has restricted access to the beach as well as restricting views. ** [AO4] **

Mappleton shows how costs vs benefits operate on coastal management. Most of the schemes employed are hard engineered but these raise a number of issues. ** [AO4] **Mappleton is at risk of collapsing into the sea and access to the beach was impossible and houses in Cliff Road were collapsing. ** [AO3]  **As a small village, the cost of protecting it was considered too much, but pressure from the local residents meant that a £2.1 million scheme was implemented. ** [AO3] **The scheme included two rock groynes designed to trap sand to increase beach depth and slow wave velocity. ** [AO3] **The cliffs were regraded and reduced slumping, along with renourishing the beach. ** [AO4] ** Finally a new road and car park were built for visitors. However, this has proved insufficient and Mappleton is still eroding. ** [AO4] ** This has led to further conflict between residents and the council on coastal management of the village.  **[AO4] **

Soft engineering is more sustainable and environmentally friendly, but it may not provide enough protection during extreme storms. **[AO4]**

Overall, hard engineering is effective in protecting specific high-value areas, while soft engineering is more sustainable in the long term. **[AO4]** The most effective coastal management usually combines both approaches. **[AO4]**

parts.problemMd: Analyse the importance of conserving coastal ecosystems compared with developing coastal areas for economic gain.
parts.solutionMd:
Conserving coastal ecosystems is very important because they provide natural protection and long-term benefits to coastal communities. **[AO3]**  Figure 2d shows that coral reefs reduce 97% of wave energy, acting as a natural barrier against storms and reducing coastal flooding. **[AO4]** This protection helps safeguard homes, infrastructure and lives, making conservation essential in areas vulnerable to storms and sea-level rise. **[AO3]**

Figure 2d shows that mangroves reduce wave height by 66%, which lowers the impact of storm surges and helps protect coastal settlements. **[AO4]** Conserving these ecosystems can therefore reduce the need for expensive hard engineering in the future. **[AO3]** .

However, developing coastal areas for economic gain is also important, particularly for employment and income. Figure 2c shows that tourism employs 2,000,000 people in the Caribbean islands, and healthy ocean habitats attract divers and tourists who support local economies. **[AO4]** Coastal development can raise living standards and provide vital income, especially in poorer regions. **[AO3]**

Conflict arises because development can damage the very ecosystems that provide protection. For example, clearing mangroves or damaging coral reefs to build hotels may increase short-term income but raise long-term flood risk. **[AO3]**

Overall, conserving coastal ecosystems is more important in the long term because it protects people and reduces future risks, but sustainable development is still necessary. The greatest importance lies in carefully balancing conservation with controlled economic development. **[AO3]**

parts.problemMd:
Study Figure 3c.

Analyse the influence plate margin type has on the scale of tectonic hazards. Refer to the resource in your answer

![World map displaying tectonic plates with divergent, convergent, and transform boundaries. Highlights include Nepal and New Zealand earthquakes, and Iceland and Tonga eruptions.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/3-hazardous-environments/3-1-anatomy-of-natural-hazards/assets/002-world-map-displaying-tectonic-plates-with-diverg.png)
parts.solutionMd:
Figure 3c shows that the type of plate margin strongly influences the scale and frequency of tectonic hazards, such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.

At divergent plate margins, hazards tend to be lower in explosivity but more frequent. Figure 3c shows Iceland is located on a divergent boundary and experiences volcanic eruptions with a VEI of 3, occurring around once every 25 years **[S]**. These eruptions usually produce runny lava rather than explosive ash clouds, meaning they are less dangerous to people, even though they happen relatively often** [Ap]**.

In contrast, convergent plate margins are associated with larger-scale but less frequent hazards. Figure 3c shows that Nepal lies on a convergent boundary between two continental plates and experienced a 7.8 magnitude earthquake, although this only happens about once every 100 years **[S]**. These earthquakes are powerful because pressure builds up as plates lock together before suddenly slipping** [Ap]**. Similarly, the Tonga eruption, also at a convergent margin, had a high VEI of 5, showing that convergent margins can produce very explosive and dangerous volcanic eruptions **[S][Ap]**.

Transform plate margins can also produce high-magnitude earthquakes. Figure 3c shows New Zealand experienced a 7.8 magnitude earthquake, but these occur much more frequently, around once every 3 years, due to plates grinding past each other and repeatedly sticking and slipping** [S]**.

Overall, convergent and transform margins tend to produce the largest and most dangerous hazards, while divergent margins usually create smaller-scale hazards** [Ap]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word **‘analyse**’ means that the answer needs to break down the components and make connections between the type of tectonic boundary and the impact of earthquakes.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a **'level of response'** approach. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark.
> 
> The AO focus includes AO3 Analysis **[Ap]** and AO4 Skills. **[S]**
> 
> - A top-level 3 answer ** ****[8 marks]** will include specific examples that show:
> 
>   - Application of knowledge and understanding
>   - Interpretation, analysis and evaluation of geographical information/issues
>   - Judgements supported by evidence
>   - Selection of information, skills and techniques
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be included in the answer includes:
> 
> - Shield volcano eruptions are often more frequent.
> - Composite volcanoes result in eruptions which include pyroclastic flows, lahars, lava, volcanic bombs. These eruptions are often less frequent.

> **[exam-tip]**
> To access the higher marks on analyse questions, do more than just describe what the resource shows.
> 
> Use the data to explain why patterns occur and make links between plate margin type and hazard scale. For example, instead of simply stating that a volcano is at a convergent boundary, explain how subduction leads to pressure build-up, making eruptions less frequent but more explosive, and compare this with hazards at other plate margins. Always develop each point with a clear cause–effect link using evidence from the resource.

parts.problemMd:
Study Figure 3c below

Analyse the hazard risk from this predicted distribution of tropical cyclones

![screenshot-2023-08-15-at-09-15-28](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/3-hazardous-environments/3-2-impact-of-natural-hazards/assets/010-screenshot-2023-08-15-at-09-15-28.png)
parts.solutionMd:
Figure 3c shows that the hazard risk from tropical cyclones varies across Asia and Oceania depending on both storm intensity and human vulnerability.

The figure shows tropical cyclones ranging from Category 1 to Category 5 on the Saffir–Simpson scale, with the darkest shading showing the most intense storms **[S]**. Many areas of South East Asia, such as the Philippines, Japan and coastal China, lie within zones where there is a 10% probability of a high-intensity tropical cyclone occurring in the next 10 years **[S]**. This increases hazard risk because stronger storms cause more damage through high winds, heavy rainfall and storm surges **[Ap]**.

Hazard risk is also increased where vulnerability is high. For example, the Philippines and Bangladesh have very dense coastal populations, meaning more people and property are exposed to cyclones** [Ap]**. Figure 3c also shows that these countries experience storms at certain times of year, such as September to May in Bangladesh, which concentrates the risk into specific seasons **[S]**. In contrast, areas of the Pacific Ocean with few or no islands have high storm intensity but low hazard risk because there are few people exposed **[Ap]**.

Climate change may further increase hazard risk by increasing the frequency and intensity of tropical cyclones and shifting where they occur, potentially putting new populations at risk** [Ap]**.

Overall, Figure 3c shows that the highest hazard risk occurs where intense tropical cyclones overlap with densely populated coastal regions and seasonal vulnerability **[S][Ap]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word **‘analyse**’ means that the answer needs to break down the components and make connections between the factors, which make some areas more vulnerable to tropical storms.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a **'level of response'** approach. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark.
> 
> The AO focus includes AO3 Analysis **[Ap]** and AO4 Skills. **[S]**
> 
> - A top-level 3 answer ** ****[8 marks]** will include specific examples that show:
> 
>   - Application of knowledge and understanding
>   - Interpretation, analysis and evaluation of geographical information/issues
>   - Judgements supported by evidence
>   - Selection of information, skills and techniques
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be included in the answer includes:
> 
> - Vulnerability to tropical cyclones is affected by the conditions that are needed for tropical cyclone formation.
> - Countries will be vulnerable at different times of the year, depending on their location.
> - Climate change has been linked with a higher frequency of tropical cyclones and a shift in where they are taking place. This means that there is the potential for a greater proportion of the world’s population to be at risk.
> - Hazard risk is a combination of the hazard (and its severity) and vulnerability. Many of the coastal areas in the zone, which have a high probability of a high-intensity tropical storm, have dense populations, which increases the hazard risk.

parts.solutionMd:
Figure 3c shows two volcanic eruptions from 2018 that had different impacts because of their location, eruption type and level of preparedness.

The eruption of Anak Krakatau in Indonesia had more severe impacts because it occurred in the sea and triggered a tsunami** [S]**. Figure 3c shows that this led to 429 deaths and over 14,000 injuries, as coastal communities had little warning and were highly vulnerable **[S]**. The eruption also caused the volcano to collapse, reducing its height from 338 m to 100 m, which increased the scale of the hazard [S]. Tsunamis are difficult to predict and evacuate for, meaning preparedness was limited and impacts were higher **[Ap]**.

In contrast, the eruption of Volcán de Fuego in Guatemala caused 190 deaths, which is lower than Anak Krakatau, despite being on land and close to settlements **[S]**. The main hazards were pyroclastic flows and ash, which destroyed villages and disrupted transport routes **[Ap]**. However, Figure 3c shows that 4,000 people were evacuated, suggesting better preparedness and emergency response helped to reduce casualties **[S][Ap]**. Ash also reached Guatemala City and closed the international airport, showing impacts over a wide area but not necessarily causing high death rates **[Ap]**.

Overall, the different impacts were caused by differences in hazard type, location and preparedness. Anak Krakatau’s tsunami led to sudden and deadly impacts, while evacuation reduced deaths at Volcán de Fuego **[Ap][S]**.

parts.problemMd: Using a named tectonic hazard event you have studied, analyse the impacts of that event on people and the environment.
parts.solutionMd:
The 2015 Nepal earthquake measured 7.8 on the Richter scale and struck Barpak village, 60 km north-west of the capital Kathmandu. **[K]** The earthquake occurred at a collision plate where Indian plate collides with the Eurasian plate, causing a release of energy. **[K]**

The impacts on people were severe. Approximately 8,600 people were killed, and over 19,000 were injured. **[U]** Nepal is a low-income country with poorly constructed buildings, which meant structures collapsed easily under the seismic shaking, with over** **600,000 homes destroyed and over 250,000** **damaged.**[U]** Hospitals were destroyed at the moment they were most needed, making it difficult to treat the injured. **[U]**

The environmental impacts were also significant.  The UNESCO World Heritage site Changu Narayan Temple and Dharahara Tower were destroyed. Widespread liquefaction occurred, where saturated soils lost their strength and behaved like liquid, destroying foundations. **[U]** Landslides were triggered in the mountainous areas, and the village of Ghodatabela was covered, leading to 250 deaths as well as blocking roads used by aid workers. **[U]**

Analysing these impacts, the level of development was the key factor in making them so devastating. A wealthier country with stricter building codes would have experienced far fewer deaths from the same magnitude earthquake. **[Ap] **The environmental and human impacts were therefore made significantly worse by Nepal's vulnerability rather than purely by the physical force of the event itself. **[Ap]**

parts.problemMd:

Analyse possible reasons why some countries are more vulnerable to the impact of earthquakes.

Refer to the resources in your answer.

![World map showing annual deaths by seismic hazards (2010-2020), highlighting USA, Mexico, and Indonesia. Colour key: grey to black for fatalities.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/3-hazardous-environments/3-2-impact-of-natural-hazards/assets/004-world-map-showing-annual-deaths-by-seismic-hazar.png)

![Table summarising earthquakes: Mexico 2017, magnitude 7.1, 370 deaths; USA 2019, magnitude 6.4, 1 death; Indonesia 2021, magnitude 6.2, 105 deaths.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/3-hazardous-environments/3-2-impact-of-natural-hazards/assets/005-table-summarising-earthquakes-mexico-2017-magnit.png)
parts.solutionMd:
Figures 3c and 3d show that vulnerability to earthquakes varies between countries due to differences in wealth, preparedness, location and governance.

One key reason is the level of economic development. Figure 3d shows that the USA (California) has a very high GDP per capita of \$65,297 and experienced only 1 death from a 6.4 magnitude earthquake **[S]**. In contrast, Indonesia and Mexico have much lower GDP per capita and have suffered far higher deaths and injuries **[S]**. Wealthier countries can afford earthquake-resistant buildings, early warning systems and well-funded emergency services, which reduce vulnerability **[Ap]**.

Healthcare capacity also affects vulnerability. Figure 3d shows Indonesia has only 0.4 doctors per 1,000 people, compared to 2.9 in the USA **[S]**. This means injuries are more likely to become fatal, increasing vulnerability after an earthquake** [Ap]**. Mexico’s higher deaths and injuries can also be linked to more limited healthcare compared to richer countries **[Ap]**.

Governance and corruption play a role. Figure 3d shows that Mexico and Indonesia have lower Corruption Perception Index scores, meaning higher perceived corruption** [S]**. This can lead to poorly enforced building regulations and unsafe construction, increasing deaths when earthquakes occur **[Ap]**.

Finally, location and population exposure increase vulnerability. Figure 3c shows higher average annual earthquake deaths in regions such as Mexico and Indonesia **[S]**. Figure 3d shows that the Mexico earthquake occurred near a large city, while the US earthquake was in a remote desert, reducing exposure **[S][Ap]**.

Overall, Figure 3d shows that even when earthquakes are of a similar magnitude, countries with higher levels of development, stronger governance and better healthcare systems experience far fewer deaths, confirming that vulnerability is shaped more by human and economic factors than by the hazard itself **[Ap][S]**.** **

![Two images show farming in Indonesia near a volcano and geothermal energy in Iceland. A table highlights views on living near volcanoes in New Zealand, Italy, and Papua New Guinea.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/3-hazardous-environments/3-2-impact-of-natural-hazards/assets/002-two-images-show-farming-in-indonesia-near-a-volc.png)
parts.solutionMd:
Figures 3c and 3d show that people continue to live in areas prone to volcanic eruptions for a range of economic, social and cultural reasons, despite the risks involved.

One important reason is economic benefit. Figure 3c shows subsistence farming taking place on fertile volcanic soils in Indonesia **[S]**. Volcanic ash creates very fertile land, allowing farmers to grow crops successfully and earn a living **[Ap]**. Figure 3c also shows geothermal energy production in Iceland, where volcanoes provide a reliable source of energy and employment **[S]**. These benefits make living near volcanoes worthwhile for many people **[Ap]**.

Employment linked to tourism is another factor. Figure 3d shows a tourism guide in Italy who lives near Mount Etna because it provides income for their family **[S]**. Volcanic landscapes attract visitors, creating jobs that are difficult to replace elsewhere** [Ap]**.

However, economic necessity is the most important reason why people continue to live near volcanoes. Figure 3d shows a fisherman in Papua New Guinea explaining that they cannot afford to move elsewhere **[S]**. For poorer communities, there is often no alternative place to live or work, meaning volcanic risk is accepted as part of daily life** [Ap]**.

In contrast, wealthier countries such as New Zealand manage volcanic risk through prediction and prevention, making the danger feel more acceptable **[S][Ap]**. Overall, while income and tradition matter, lack of choice due to poverty is the most significant factor keeping people living in hazardous volcanic areas **[Ap]**.

Analyse the use of hazard, vulnerability and risk mapping in reducing the impact  of earthquakes.
parts.solutionMd:
Hazard, vulnerability and risk mapping are important tools for reducing the impacts of earthquakes by improving planning, response and long-term management.

Before an earthquake, hazard mapping helps identify areas most likely to be affected based on past events and physical geography. Figure 3c shows that data is collected and used to produce hazard maps, which can then be shared with emergency planners and other organisations **[S].** These maps allow governments to plan land-use zoning and enforce earthquake-resistant building regulations in high-risk areas, reducing future damage **[Ap]**. Vulnerability maps also show where populations and infrastructure are most at risk, helping to prioritise preparedness **[Ap][S]**.

During and immediately after an earthquake, hazard and risk maps support emergency response. Figure 3c shows that maps can be used in the field to coordinate relief efforts, such as deciding where to send food, medical aid and heavy equipment **[S]**. Roads and key infrastructure identified on hazard maps allow relief teams to reach affected areas more quickly, reducing loss of life **[Ap]**. Sharing maps across agencies helps avoid duplication and ensures resources are not wasted **[Ap]**.

Figure 3d shows a clear relationship between hazard, vulnerability and risk **[S]**. Areas with high hazard often also have high vulnerability, leading to high risk **[Ap]**. However, some areas have high hazard but only moderate vulnerability, meaning risk is lower, showing how mapping helps target support more effectively **[S][Ap]**.

Overall, hazard, vulnerability and risk mapping reduce earthquake impacts by improving preparedness, enabling faster responses and guiding long-term risk reduction **[Ap]**.

GIS helps reduce this initial deterioration by improving emergency response **[Ap]**. Figure 3d shows that GIS teams first collect data on roads, buildings and local services before the disaster **[S]**. This means planners already understand the area at risk and can respond more quickly when an earthquake occurs **[Ap]**.

After the earthquake, GIS is used to present and share data, often as maps, with emergency services and support agencies **[S]**. These maps help identify damaged areas and blocked roads, allowing emergency aid to reach affected communities faster **[Ap]**. This speeds up search, rescue and care, helping quality of life begin to recover sooner, as shown in Figure 3c **[S][Ap]**. Sharing GIS maps also ensures relief efforts are coordinated, so resources are not wasted or sent to the wrong locations** [Ap]**.

In the longer term, Figure 3d shows that GIS can be used in assessment and in the field to plan recovery and reconstruction** [S]**. GIS helps planners decide where services were before and where new housing or infrastructure should be built more safely **[Ap]**. Overall, GIS reduces earthquake risk by improving preparedness, response and recovery, helping communities recover more quickly and effectively** [Ap]**.

Finally, evacuation plans and emergency services help reduce risk. Figure 3c shows designated evacuation routes, shelters and well-trained emergency services **[S]**. This allows a faster and more organised response after an earthquake **[Ap]**.

This increases awareness and ensures people know what to do during an earthquake, reducing panic and casualties** [Ap]**. Schools and workplaces running drills further improve this response **[Ap]**.

parts.problemMd: Explain how rural-urban migration can lead to the growth of informal employment in megacities.
parts.solutionMd:
Rural-urban migration brings large numbers of people into megacities such as Lagos or Mumbai in search of work. **[1]** However, the formal economy cannot absorb all new arrivals quickly enough, leaving many people without official jobs. **[1]** As a result, migrants turn to informal work, such as street trading, waste picking, or domestic labour, to survive. **[1]** This creates a large informal sector because the supply of labour far exceeds the number of formal jobs available, and many migrants lack the qualifications or contacts needed to enter formal employment. **[1]**

![fig-1c-4ge1-02-june-2019-edexcel-igcse-geography](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/4-economic-activity-and-energy/4-1-economic-sectors/assets/012-fig-1c-4ge1-02-june-2019-edexcel-igcse-geography.png)

Analyse the reasons for changes in primary and quaternary employment.
parts.solutionMd:
Figure 1c shows clear changes in **primary** and **quaternary** employment as countries move from pre-industrial to post-industrial stages of development **[S]**.

Primary employment involves working with natural resources such as farming, fishing and mining. Figure 1c shows that in the pre-industrial stage, primary employment is very high, at around 70%** [AO4]**. This is because developing economies rely heavily on agriculture for income and food, meaning most people must work in the primary sector to meet basic needs, which explains why primary employment is dominant at this stage **[AO3]**. During the industrial stage, Figure 1c shows the steepest decline in primary employment **[AO4]**. This happens as mechanisation reduces the need for farm labour and people migrate to urban areas for industrial jobs, leading to a rapid fall in primary sector employment **[AO3]**. In the post-industrial stage, Figure 1c shows that primary employment continues to decline but at a slower rate, reaching around 10%, as advanced economies depend less on natural resource extraction **[AO4][AO3]**.

Quaternary employment includes information technology, research and development and universities. Figure 1c shows that quaternary employment starts from almost 0% and only grows in the post-industrial stage, reaching about 5% **[AO4]**. This growth occurs because increased wealth allows governments and businesses to invest in education, ICT and scientific research, creating demand for highly skilled, knowledge-based jobs and explaining why quaternary employment rises only at later stages of development **[AO3]**. However, Figure 1c also shows that quaternary employment remains relatively low overall, as these specialist jobs require advanced skills and infrastructure **[AO4][AO3]**.

Overall, Figure 1c shows that economic development, technological change and rising wealth explain the decline in primary employment and the growth of quaternary employment over time** [AO3][AO4]**.

Figure 1c shows that countries have very different employment structures, which can mainly be explained by their level of economic development and how closely they follow the Clark–Fisher model.

Burundi has a very high proportion of primary sector employment, at over 80%, and very low tertiary employment **[AO4]**. This suggests Burundi is at a pre-industrial stage of development. This is because low-income countries rely heavily on farming and raw materials for jobs, as there is little industry or service employment available, meaning most people work in the primary sector **[AO3]**.

In contrast, Canada has a very low proportion of primary employment and a very high proportion of tertiary and quaternary employment, at around 80%, as well as a very high GDP per capita of \$51,987 **[AO4]**. This shows Canada is a post-industrial economy. High levels of education, technology and investment create more service and knowledge-based jobs, which explains why most people work in the tertiary and quaternary sectors **[AO3]**.

Countries such as Mexico, Nigeria and Liberia show more mixed employment structures** [AO4]**. Mexico has a balanced mix of secondary and tertiary employment, while Nigeria and Liberia have higher tertiary employment than Burundi, despite lower GDP per capita **[AO4]**. This suggests countries do not all develop at the same speed or in the same way, as factors such as education, resources and government priorities can affect employment patterns **[AO3]**.

Overall, the level of economic development is the most important factor explaining the differences in employment structure. Figure 1c shows a clear pattern where developing countries have high primary employment, while developed countries are dominated by tertiary and quaternary jobs, confirming the Clark–Fisher model** [AO3][AO4]**.

parts.problemMd:
Study Figure 1c.

Analyse reasons for changes in the employment sectors shown. Refer to the resource in your answer.

![Graph of Clark-Fisher model showing employment sector trends: primary declines, secondary peaks and decreases, tertiary and quaternary rise over time.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/4-economic-activity-and-energy/4-1-economic-sectors/assets/003-graph-of-clark-fisher-model-showing-employment-s.png)
parts.solutionMd:
Figure 1c shows the Clark–Fisher model, which explains how employment sectors typically change as a country develops over time.

In the pre-industrial stage, Figure 1c shows that the primary sector dominates, accounting for around 70% of employment **[AO4]**. This is because economies at this stage rely heavily on agriculture and extraction for food and income. Limited technology means farming is labour-intensive, so most people work in the primary sector **[AO3]**.

During the industrial stage, Figure 1c shows a sharp decline in primary employment and a rise in secondary and tertiary employment** [AO4]**. Mechanisation of agriculture reduces the need for farm workers, pushing people to move to cities for factory jobs, causing rural–urban migration. As factories grow, services such as transport, retail and banking are also needed, which explains the growth of the tertiary sector alongside the secondary sector **[AO3]**.

In the post-industrial stage, Figure 1c shows that tertiary employment becomes dominant, reaching over 50%, while the secondary sector declines and the quaternary sector begins to grow** [AO4]**. This happens because manufacturing is increasingly automated or moved overseas, while demand grows for services such as education, healthcare, ICT and research. Advances in technology reduce factory labour but create knowledge-based jobs **[AO3]**.

Overall, the most important reason for the changes in employment sectors is economic development. Figure 1c shows that as countries develop, employment shifts from primary to secondary and then towards tertiary and quaternary sectors, confirming the Clark–Fisher model** [AO3][AO4].**

Malthus argued that population grows faster than food supply, meaning that eventually resources will run out and population will crash through famine, disease, or war. **[1] **Boserup disagreed, arguing that human ingenuity means that when population pressure increases, people find new ways to produce more food through technological innovation. **[1]** The key difference is that Malthus saw population growth as a crisis, whereas Boserup saw it as a driver of progress. **[1]**

Analyse the reasons for the patterns of informal employment.

Refer to the resource in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Figure 1c shows clear global patterns in informal employment, with much higher levels in developing regions compared to more developed ones. Informal employment refers to work that is unregulated, unofficial and untaxed, such as street vending or casual labour **[AO3]**.

In regions such as Africa (71.9%), the Middle East (68.6%) and Asia and the Pacific (68.2%), informal employment makes up over two thirds of all jobs **[AO4]**. One reason for this is rapid rural–urban migration. Large numbers of people move to cities in search of work, but there are not enough formal jobs available, so many people are forced to work informally to earn an income **[AO3]**. In addition, wages in formal employment in these regions are often low, meaning family members may take on informal work to supplement household income **[AO3]**.

In contrast, Europe and Central Asia have much lower levels of informal employment, at around 20.8%, with formal work making up 79.2% **[AO4]**. This is because these regions contain many developed countries with stricter employment laws, better enforcement and more formal job opportunities, so less informal employment exists **[AO3]**. The Americas also show lower informal employment (40%) compared to Africa and Asia, reflecting higher levels of economic development in countries such as the USA and Canada** [AO4]**.

Overall, Figure 1c shows that informal employment is unevenly distributed and is strongly linked to levels of development, with poorer regions relying more heavily on informal work** [AO3]**.

parts.problemMd: Analyse the extent to which Boserup's theory provides a more convincing explanation of the relationship between population growth and resources than Malthus's theory.
parts.solutionMd:
Malthus argued that population grows faster than food supply, so eventually resources will be unable to support the population.** [K]** He predicted that 'positive checks', such as famine, disease, and war, would control population growth when resources ran out. **[K]** This was a pessimistic view that saw population growth as a problem with no human solution.** [U]**

Boserup offered a different view, arguing that necessity is the mother of invention. **[K]** When population grows and food becomes scarce, people develop new technologies and farming methods to increase food production. **[K] **Examples include the development of irrigation, the Green Revolution, and high-yield crop varieties, all of which have allowed food production to keep pace with population growth. **[U]** This suggests that human ingenuity can overcome resource limits, making Boserup's theory more optimistic and arguably more consistent with what has actually happened in the world since Malthus wrote in 1798. **[Ap]**

However, Malthus's theory does have some merit. **[Ap]** Food insecurity and famine in sub-Saharan Africa persist despite technological advances **[K]**, suggesting that resources do not always keep pace with population. **[U]** This supports the Malthusian idea that population growth can exceed supply. **[Ap]**

Since global food production has grown with population, Boserup's theory does seem more plausible. **[U] **But there is no single theory that explains the population-resource relationship, because it varies by location and level of development. **[Ap]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**analyse**' means that the answer needs to examine the evidence for each theory, make connections between ideas, and reach a reasoned judgement. The examiner expects the answer to weigh up the two theories against each other.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a level of response approach. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark.
> 
> A top-level Level 3** ****[7–8 marks]**** **answer will**:**
> 
> - **AO1 ****[K]**: show knowledge of the Malthusian and Boserupian theories and relevant examples
> - **AO2** **[U]**: show understanding of how the theories explain the relationship between population and resources, and how they compare
> - **AO3 ****[Ap]**: apply knowledge and understanding to reach a reasoned judgement about which theory is more convincing
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question, as it will depend on the examples used. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Wealthier countries tend to reflect Boserupian outcomes; poorer regions can reflect Malthusian pressures
> - Malthus's theory is relevant where development levels are low and technology has not reached all communities
> - Any other appropriate response
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Writing about one theory makes a balanced analysis impossible
> - Treating 'analyse' as 'describe'. Analysis requires connections, comparisons, and judgement

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Avoid** writing a long introduction to avoid running out of time before reaching a judgement. Get to the comparison quickly.
> 
> **Keep** an eye on your word count. At roughly 20 to 25 words per minute, you have around 9 to 11 minutes for this question. Use every second of it.

parts.problemMd:
Study Figure 1c.

Analyse the reasons for differences in the energy mix of these two regions.

You must refer to the resource in your answer.

![Two pie charts compare the 2020 energy mix of Africa and the EU; Africa relies on gas, while the EU uses oil significantly more.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/4-economic-activity-and-energy/4-3-energy---production-security-and-management/assets/003-two-pie-charts-compare-the-2020-energy-mix-of-af.png)
parts.solutionMd:
Figure 1c shows the energy mix of Africa and the European Union. Although both regions use similar types of energy, there are clear differences in the proportions used. These differences are mainly due to natural resources, levels of development and investment in energy infrastructure. **[AO3]**

One reason for the different energy mixes is the availability of natural resources. Africa uses a much higher proportion of hydropower (17%) compared to the EU (7%), as shown in Figure 1c **[AO4]**. This is because Africa has large river systems such as the Congo and Nile, which are suitable for hydroelectric power. The EU has fewer large rivers, so it relies less on hydropower. This shows how physical geography affects the energy mix. **[AO3]**

Another reason is differences in economic development and investment. The EU uses far more nuclear energy (10%) than Africa (1%) **[AO4]**. Nuclear power requires high levels of investment and advanced technology, which the EU can afford. Many African countries lack the money and infrastructure needed, so nuclear makes up a much smaller share of their energy mix. **[AO3]**

Energy demand also explains differences. Both regions rely heavily on gas (Africa 40%, EU 35%) **[AO4]**, but the EU uses more oil (31%) than Africa (15%) [AO4]. This is due to higher industrial activity and transport use in the EU. Africa’s lower energy demand reduces reliance on oil.** [AO3]**

Overall, differences in development and investment are the most important reasons for the contrasting energy mixes between Africa and the EU.

> - Investment in renewable energy technologies can be expensive.

parts.problemMd:
Study Figure 1c.

Analyse the possible reasons for changes in global energy consumption.

You must refer to the resource in your answer

![Stacked area chart showing global fossil fuel consumption from 1981 to 2021 in TWh, with gas, oil, and coal usage each increasing over time.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/4-economic-activity-and-energy/4-3-energy---production-security-and-management/assets/002-stacked-area-chart-showing-global-fossil-fuel-co.png)
parts.solutionMd:
Figure 1c shows global energy consumption from fossil fuels between 1981 and 2021. Overall, fossil fuel use has increased over time, although there are some small decreases. These changes can be explained by population growth, industrialisation and continued reliance on fossil fuels. **[AO3]**

One reason for the increase in global energy consumption is population growth. As the world’s population has grown, more energy is needed for homes, transport and electricity. Figure 1c shows that total fossil fuel consumption has risen steadily from 1981 to 2021 **[AO4]**. Many countries cannot meet this demand using renewable energy alone, so fossil fuels are still widely used. This explains the overall upward trend shown in the resource. **[AO3]**

Another reason is industrialisation in developing and emerging countries. Figure 1c shows coal use increasing from around 20,000 TWh in 1981 to over 40,000 TWh in 2021 **[AO4]**. Coal is often used because it is cheap and reliable, especially in countries such as China and India. As factories and industries grow, energy demand increases, leading to higher fossil fuel consumption. **[AO3]**

Despite pressure to reduce emissions, many countries still depend on fossil fuels for energy security. Figure 1c shows gas use increasing its share over time **[AO4]**. However, there are small drops around 2010 and 2020, possibly due to economic slowdown and the COVID-19 pandemic. **[AO3]**

Overall, population growth and industrialisation are the main reasons for the increase in global energy consumption, although concern about climate change may slow future growth.

parts.problemMd:
Study Figure 2c below.

![fig-2c-4ge1-02-june-2019-edexcel-igcse-geography](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/5-rural-environments/5-1-the-worlds-biomes/assets/007-fig-2c-4ge1-02-june-2019-edexcel-igcse-geography.png)

Analyse how exploiting natural ecosystems can affect their goods and services.
parts.solutionMd:
Figure 2c shows four types of ecosystem goods and services: provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural. Exploiting natural ecosystems can increase the supply of some goods in the short term, but it can also damage services, reducing the long-term benefits ecosystems provide.

One way exploitation affects ecosystems is through increasing provisioning goods such as food and fuel. Figure 2c shows provisioning services including food, biomass fuel and freshwater **[AO4]**. For example, forests may be cleared for farming to increase food production. While this can increase food supply and support development, it can also reduce other ecosystem functions, which means it is not sustainable in the long term. **[AO3]**

Exploitation can also reduce regulating services. Figure 2c shows regulating services such as climate regulation, erosion control and water run-off **[AO4].** When ecosystems like forests are exploited through logging, carbon storage decreases and soil erosion increases. Overall, exploiting natural ecosystems can increase some goods temporarily, but it often damages services, meaning long-term environmental and human benefits are reduced.

parts.problemMd:
Study Figure 2c which shows the world's biomes

Analyse the reasons for the distribution of the world's biomes

![screenshot-2023-07-27-at-09-39-12](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/5-rural-environments/5-1-the-worlds-biomes/assets/004-screenshot-2023-07-27-at-09-39-12.png)
parts.solutionMd:
Figure 2c shows the global distribution of the world’s biomes. Biomes are large-scale ecosystems such as deserts, tropical rainforests and tundra. Their distribution is mainly controlled by climate, especially temperature and rainfall, although other factors also influence the pattern.

The most important reason for the distribution of biomes is latitude and climate. Figure 2c shows tropical rainforests found near the Equator, where temperatures are high and rainfall is heavy all year **[AO4].** In contrast, tundra is found in high-latitude areas such as northern Canada and Russia, where temperatures are very low. This shows that temperature and precipitation strongly control which biome can exist in each region. **[AO3]**

Rainfall patterns also help explain biome distribution. Figure 2c shows deserts in areas such as North Africa and central Australia **[AO4]**. These regions receive very little rainfall, making it difficult for vegetation to grow. Areas with seasonal rainfall often have grassland or savanna biomes, while places with year-round rainfall support forests. This shows how different climate conditions create different biomes. **[AO3]**

Local factors such as altitude can disrupt the global pattern. Figure 2c shows mountain ranges like the Andes, Himalayas and Rockies **[AO4]**. At high altitudes, temperatures are lower, so biomes such as taiga and tundra can be found even near the Equator. Human activity can also change vegetation locally, although this is not shown clearly on the map.** [AO3]**

Overall, climate linked to latitude is the main reason for the distribution of the world’s biomes, but altitude and local factors can also affect the pattern.

parts.problemMd:

Analyse the importance of natural ecosystems for the provision of goods.

You must refer to the resource in your answer.

![Diagram illustrating ecosystem benefits, split into goods and services, including water supply, tourism, food, habitats, climate regulation, and health.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/5-rural-environments/5-1-the-worlds-biomes/assets/002-diagram-illustrating-ecosystem-benefits-split-in.jpeg)
parts.solutionMd:
Figure 2c shows the range of goods and services provided by natural ecosystems. Ecosystem goods are physical products such as food and water, while services are benefits that support human wellbeing. Natural ecosystems are important because both goods and services work together to support human life and economic activity.

One important ecosystem good is food and drink. Figure 2c shows that ecosystems provide food and drink as a key good **[AO4]**. Ecosystems such as forests, oceans and grasslands supply crops, fish and meat. Without healthy ecosystems, food production would decrease, showing how important these goods are for human survival. **[AO3]**

Water supply is another important ecosystem good. Figure 2c shows water supply as a key good provided by ecosystems **[AO4]**. Rivers, lakes and wetlands store and filter water naturally, making it suitable for drinking and farming. This also links to services such as water and nutrient cycling, which help maintain water quality.** [AO3]**

Although goods are important, ecosystems also provide many services that support the supply of goods. Figure 2c shows services such as carbon storage, flood management and habitats for species **[AO4]**. These services protect ecosystems and allow goods like food and materials to be produced. For example, forests store carbon and reduce flooding, helping to protect farmland.** [AO3]**

Overall, although goods are important, services are necessary to maintain ecosystems. The value of services is not as easy to calculate, but without them, the goods would not be available.

parts.problemMd:
Study Figure 2c.

Analyse the factors that affect the structure of rural populations in developing countries.

Refer to the resource in your answer.

![Population pyramid of Nigeria 2019, showing urban and rural age distribution. Dark blue for rural and light blue for urban areas.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-geography-19/5-rural-environments/5-2-characteristics-of-rural-environments/assets/008-population-pyramid-of-nigeria-2019-showing-urban.png)
parts.solutionMd:
Figure 2c shows the population structure of Nigeria in 2019, comparing rural and urban populations. The structure of rural populations in developing countries is affected mainly by human factors such as migration, employment opportunities and access to services. These factors influence which groups remain in rural areas.

One key factor affecting rural population structure is rural–urban migration. Figure 2c shows that there is a much smaller proportion of people aged 20–24 living in rural areas (around 3%) compared to urban areas (around 6%)** [AO4]**. This age group is the economically active group (working age) and often moves to cities for jobs, education and better living conditions. As a result, rural areas lose working-age adults, changing the population structure.** [AO3]**

Another factor is high birth rates in rural areas. Figure 2c shows a large proportion of young children aged 0–4 and 5–9 in rural areas** [AO4]**. This is partly due to limited access to healthcare and family planning, as well as cultural preferences for larger families. Many children stay in rural areas because they are too young to migrate, increasing the proportion of young dependents. **[AO3]**

Finally, limited services and job opportunities affect who remains in rural areas. Older people are more likely to stay because they depend on farming and family support. This leads to an ageing population alongside many young children, creating a dependent population structure.** [AO3]**

Overall, rural–urban migration is the most important factor shaping rural population structure, as it removes working-age adults and leaves behind younger and older age groups.

parts.solutionMd:
Figure 2c shows changes in the urban and rural population of Brazil between 1950 and 2050. Rural areas in developing and emerging countries are changing mainly due to human factors such as migration, economic development and globalisation.

One major factor leading to change in rural areas is rural–urban migration. Figure 2c shows that in 1950, around two-thirds of Brazil’s population lived in rural areas, but by 2020, around 90% lived in urban areas** [AO4]**. People move to cities for better job opportunities, education and healthcare. This leads to rural areas losing economically active adults, leaving behind an ageing population and fewer workers. **[AO3]**

Another factor is the decline of traditional rural employment. Figure 2c shows that after around 2000, the rural population began to slowly decline **[AO4]**. As agriculture becomes more mechanised, fewer workers are needed. This can reduce agricultural output and income in rural areas. As a result, some rural communities diversify by developing tourism or switching to higher-value crops that need less labour. **[AO3]**

Globalisation also affects rural areas. Figure 2c shows overall population growth, mainly in urban areas** [AO4]**. Investment and economic growth are often focused on cities. This causes rural areas to be neglected, leading to fewer services and opportunities, encouraging further migration.** [AO3]**

Overall, rural–urban migration caused by economic development is the most important factor changing rural areas, as it reduces population, labour supply and long-term sustainability.

Many people migrate from rural to urban areas for better-paid jobs, leaving fewer workers available for farming. This means farmers may need to hire seasonal or migrant workers, changing how farms operate. **[AO3]**

Another factor is pressure on rural land from counter-urbanisation. Figure 2c shows that a property company tried to buy farmland to build houses **[AO4]**. This happens because people want to live in rural areas while working in cities. As a result, farmland may be sold for housing or business use, reducing agricultural land and changing the rural landscape. **[AO3]**

Economic pressures on farming also lead to change. Figure 2c shows that the farmer opened a farm shop with a coffee shop to make more money **[AO4]**. Falling crop prices due to cheap imports mean farming alone is often not profitable. Farmers diversify into tourism or retail to remain viable. **[AO3]**

Overall, economic pressures are the most important factor driving rural change in developed countries, as they influence labour availability, land use and the need for diversification.

Analyse the factors that are leading to changes in rural areas in developed countries.
