parts.problemMd:
You have studied river environments as part of your own geographical enquiry.

Evaluate the accuracy and reliability of the conclusion you drew from your enquiry.

State the title of your geographical enquiry.
parts.solutionMd:
'How does pebble roundness change downstream along the River Wye?'

I came to the conclusion that pebble roundness increases as you move downstream as erosion smooths pebbles as they are transported. **[K]** Overall, my data primarily supports this conclusion, but some accuracy and reliability issues make me less confident. **[Ap]**

The main method I used to collect data was the Power's Scale. I compared each pebble to a visual chart to assign it a roundness score between 1 and 6. **[E] **This method is subjective because different students may judge the same pebble differently. **[Ap]** This reduces accuracy because scores depend on the measurer rather than a precise instrument. **[Ap]**

To improve reliability, I measured ten pebbles at each site and calculated the median. **[E]** A median reduced the impact of outliers like Site 6's 4 score. **[Ap]** Ten pebbles is a small sample. A larger sample of twenty pebbles per site would have improved median reliability. **[Ap]**

I found that the median score increased from 2.5 at Site 1 to 5.5 at Site 6, supporting the erosion theory. **[E]** This consistency across all six sites supports my conclusion. **[Ap]**

However, the subjectivity of the Power's Scale means individual readings may not be accurate. A calliper measurement of roundness would improve accuracy in the future. **[Ap]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**evaluate**' means the answer must consider the strengths and limitations of the enquiry across more than one stage of the enquiry process and must reach a clear overall judgement.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a level of response approach. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark.
> 
> A top-level 3 answer **[8 marks]** will include specific examples that show:
> 
> - **AO1**: **[K]** knowledge about fieldwork methods, river processes and the enquiry context
> - **AO3**: **[Ap]** application of knowledge to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of data and to assess the validity of the conclusion
> - **AO4**: **[E]** use of specific evidence from the student's own enquiry to support evaluative judgements
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question and will depend on the example used. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Evaluation of the sampling method used (systematic, random or stratified) and whether it produced a representative sample of pebbles
> - Discussion of whether the number of sites was sufficient to draw a reliable conclusion about the whole river
> - Reference to secondary data sources such as Environment Agency records or OS maps and how these supported or challenged the primary data
> - Evaluation of data presentation choices and whether they clearly showed the downstream trend
> - Any weather or environmental conditions on the fieldwork day that may have affected the data collected
> - Discussion of the difference between accuracy (how close to the true value) and reliability (how repeatable) with specific reference to the student's own methods
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Writing only about data collection
> - Confusing accuracy with reliability
> - Describing fieldwork rather than assessing its impact on the conclusion
> - Not including an overall judgement
> - Writing about coastal or hazardous environments fieldwork

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Know **the difference between accuracy and reliability before you enter the exam room.
> 
> - **Accuracy** asks: are my results close to the true value?
> - **Reliability **asks: if I repeated this, would I get the same results?
> - Use both words correctly and link them to specific parts of your own enquiry.
> 
> **A clear** overall judgement at the end is essential for Level 3. It does not need to be long. One sentence that directly answers whether and why your conclusion was accurate and reliable.

parts.solutionMd:
Arrange the six values in order from smallest to largest:

*27, 38, 49, 57, 61, 68*

parts.problemMd:
You have studied coastal environments as part of your own geographical enquiry.

Evaluate the accuracy and reliability of the conclusion you drew from your enquiry.

State the title of your geographical enquiry.
parts.solutionMd:
'How does sediment size change along Chesil Beach from west to east?'

I concluded that sediment size decreases from west to east because longshore drift transports and sorts material, with smaller pebbles carried furthest by south-westerly waves. **[K]** Generally, my data supports this conclusion, but some sites' accuracy and reliability issues limit my confidence. **[Ap]**

A ruler was used to measure the long axis of ten pebbles at each site for my main data collection. **[K]** This simple method is error-prone. Different students may have measured the pebble differently, picking the longest or widest axis. **[Ap]** Inconsistent technique can distort pebble length measurements. **[Ap]**

Instead of picking pebbles by hand, we used systematic sampling to improve reliability. **[K] **This reduced the risk of bias, where students unconsciously chose larger or more interesting pebbles. **[Ap]** However, ten pebbles per site is a small sample, and using twenty would have produced a more reliable median. **[Ap]**

Site 4's anomaly slightly influenced my conclusion. **[K]** I identified it as possibly caused by a nearby groyne trapping sediment, confirming the trend rather than poor data collection. **[Ap]**

My conclusion was strengthened by secondary data from the British Geological Survey that confirmed the eastern end of the beach has much finer sediment than the western end. **[Ap]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**evaluate**' means the answer must consider the strengths and limitations of the enquiry across more than one stage of the enquiry process and must reach a clear overall judgement.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a level of response approach. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark.
> 
> A top-level 3 answer **[8 marks]** will include specific examples that show:
> 
> - **AO1**: **[K]**  knowledge about coastal processes, fieldwork methods and the enquiry context
> - **AO3**: **[Ap]** application of knowledge to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of data and to assess the validity of the conclusion
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question and will depend on the example used. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Assessing whether the sampling strategy produced a representative sediment sample at each site
> - Evaluation if enough sites were available to draw reliable conclusions about the beach
> - Use of OS maps, BGS records, and Environment Agency coastal monitoring data to support or challenge primary data
> - Decisions on data presentation and whether graphs showed sediment size trends
> - How recent storm activity or unusually calm weather may have affected sediment distribution on the day

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Know **the difference between accuracy and reliability.
> 
> - **Accuracy** asks: are my results close to the true value?
> - **Reliability **asks: if I repeated this, would I get the same results?
> - Use both words correctly and link them to specific parts of your own enquiry.

parts.problemMd:
A student investigated how air temperature varies across an urban area during a heatwave. They recorded air temperature in degrees Celsius at six sites along a transect from the rural fringe to the city centre. The results are shown in the table below.

| Site | Location | Air temperature (°C) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Rural fringe | 28.4 |
| 2 | Suburban housing | 29.7 |
| 3 | Urban park | 27.1 |
| 4 | Inner suburb | 31.2 |
| 5 | City centre edge | 32.6 |
| 6 | City centre core | 33.8 |

Calculate the median air temperature recorded across the** six sites. **

Show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
First, arrange the six values in order from smallest to largest:

27.1, 28.4, 29.7, 31.2, 32.6, 33.8 **[1]**

There are 6 values, so the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th values.

3rd value = 29.7, 4th value = 31.2

Median = (29.7 + 31.2) ÷ 2 = 60.9 ÷ 2 = **30.45°C** **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**calculate**' means you must show your working and give a numerical answer.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a** point-marked** approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for correctly identifying the 3rd and 4th values as 29.7 and 31.2 after ordering the data to find the middle value
> - **One mark** for the correct final answer of 30.45°C or 30.5°C
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> - The answer 30.45 without the unit '°C' is acceptable but the unit should be encouraged
> 
> **Do not accept:**
> 
> - The mean of the six values, which gives 30.47°C
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Calculating the mean instead of the median. Students must read the command word carefully.
> - Forgetting to reorder the data before selecting the middle values, which leads to the incorrect 3rd and 4th values being used.
> - Selecting only the 3rd value rather than averaging the 3rd and 4th values in an even-numbered data set.

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Always **reorder the data before doing anything else. The values in the table are not in numerical order, and if you use them as they appear, you will get the wrong answer.
> 
> **With **six values there is no single middle number. Find the average of the 3rd and 4th values after ordering. Show every step clearly because the working earns a mark.

parts.problemMd:
You have studied hazardous environments as part of your own geographical enquiry.

Evaluate the accuracy and reliability of the conclusion you drew from your enquiry.

State the title of your geographical enquiry.
parts.solutionMd:
'To what extent did prolonged heavy rainfall increase flood risk in the River Severn catchment in February?'

I concluded that saturated soil, impermeable urban surfaces, and high antecedent rainfall combined increase flood risk because water will reach the river channel faster. **[K] **Overall my data supports this conclusion, but some sites' accuracy and reliability issues limit my confidence. **[Ap]**

I measured river levels at three catchment gauging locations using a metre rule marked at a fixed point on each bridge as my primary data collection method. **[K] **Though cheap and simple, this method proved inaccurate. The water surface level fluctuated with each flow pulse, making it difficult to get an exact reading. This caused some readings to be slightly higher or lower than the measured water level. **[Ap]**

In two minutes, I took three readings at each measuring site and used the mean to reduce the impact of any single error. **[K]** I only visited each site once a day, so I couldn't get hourly river levels, which restricted my flood response speed conclusion. **[Ap]**

Secondary Environment Agency data revealed Shrewsbury Severn River levels reached 5.2 m above average in February, supporting my hypothesis. **[K]** This similarity between my main observations and the official record confirmed my flood risk conclusion. **[Ap]**

My conclusion is reliable because my trend matched my data and secondary evidence. A longer data collecting time and digital water level logger would have improved my findings' accuracy and reliability. **[Ap]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**evaluate**' means the answer must consider the strengths and limitations of the enquiry across more than one stage of the enquiry process and must reach a clear overall judgement.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a level of response approach. Each point made in the answer does not equal a mark.
> 
> A top-level 3 answer **[8 marks]** will include specific examples that show:
> 
> - **AO1**: **[K]**  knowledge about weather hazards, flood processes, fieldwork methods and the enquiry context
> - **AO3**: **[Ap]** application of knowledge to evaluate the accuracy and reliability of data and to assess the validity of the conclusion
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question and will depend on the example used. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - How Environment Agency flood records, Met Office rainfall data, and newspaper reports supported or challenged primary data
> - Data presentation and whether graphs or maps clearly showed the rainfall-flood risk relationship
> - Discussion of how data collection timing relative to the flood peak may have affected the data recorded
> - A comparison of accuracy and reliability using the student's hazardous environments methods
> - Possible ethical or practical issues with collecting data during a flood, such as restricted access to flooded sites

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Know **the difference between accuracy and reliability.
> 
> - **Accuracy** asks: are my results close to the true value?
> - **Reliability **asks: if I repeated this, would I get the same results?
> - Use both words correctly and link them to specific parts of your own enquiry.
> 
> **A clear** overall judgement at the end is essential for Level 3. It does not need to be long. One sentence that directly answers whether and why your conclusion was accurate and reliable.
> 
> **One **final and important reminder: this question must be answered using your hazardous environments fieldwork, which must be based on an extreme weather event. Answers about tectonic hazards will score zero regardless of their quality.

parts.problemMd:
The students visited five sites in the small market town of Thornfield and recorded the number of solar panels visible on buildings.

Explain **one **risk that the students may have faced during their fieldwork in Thornfield, and describe how they could have managed it.
parts.solutionMd:
One risk was traffic when recording data near roadsides and on busy streets in the town centre. **[1]** The students could have managed this by carrying out a risk assessment before the visit, identifying the most dangerous locations in advance. **[1]** They could also have worked in pairs and stood on the pavement away from the road at all times during data collection. **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**explain**' means the answer must go beyond simply naming a risk. The answer must show how the risk was or could have been managed.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for identifying a plausible risk linked to the fieldwork context
> - **One mark** for explaining one way of managing that risk
> - **One further mark** for developing the management strategy
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> **Risks**
> 
> - Uneven or slippery surfaces at the rural fringe or industrial site
> - Adverse weather conditions during outdoor data collection
> - Working near an industrial area with potential hazards
> - Personal safety when working in pairs in unfamiliar locations
> 
> **Management strategies**
> 
> - Wearing high-visibility clothing near roads or industrial areas
> - Informing a responsible adult of the route and timing
> - Checking the weather forecast and dressing appropriately
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Naming a risk without explaining how it was managed
> - Giving a very generic risk such as 'getting lost' without linking it to the Thornfield fieldwork context
> - Describing the risk in detail but neglecting the management strategy entirely

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Structure **your answer in two clear parts:
> 
> - the risk
> - the management
> 
> **The** third mark is always for development of the management strategy, so push your answer one step further than the obvious.
> 
> **Instead **of just saying 'do a risk assessment', say what the risk assessment would identify or what action it would lead to.

The students visited five sites and recorded the number of solar panels visible on buildings. They also completed an environmental quality survey (EQS) at each site, scoring each location out of 10, where 10 represents the highest environmental quality.

|---|---|---|---|

| 4 | Rural fringe | 24 | 9 |

Using **Figure 1,** explain **one **way the students could have used secondary data to support their enquiry into changing energy use in Thornfield.
parts.solutionMd:
The students could have used local council planning records **[1]** to find out how many planning applications for solar panel installation had been approved in Thornfield over the past ten years, allowing them to compare the trend in applications with the pattern of solar panels they recorded in Figure 1. **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**explain**' means a named secondary source alone is not sufficient. The answer must show how that source would support or extend the fieldwork findings.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for identifying a specific and plausible secondary data source
> - **One mark** for explaining how it would support the enquiry into changing energy use
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Government energy statistics on renewable energy adoption by region
> - Satellite images or historic Google Maps images to track changes in solar panel numbers over time
> - Local newspaper articles reporting on energy schemes in Thornfield
> - Energy company data on households connected to renewable energy tariffs
> 
> No credit will be given for vague sources, such as 'the internet' or 'a website', without further specification.
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Naming a secondary source without explaining how it links to the enquiry focus
> - Describing primary data collection methods instead of secondary data
> - Using Figure 1 data as the secondary source (Figure 1 is primary fieldwork data)

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Secondary **data means data collected by someone else, not by you.
> 
> **Always** name the source precisely, then use the word 'because' or 'to compare' to link it to the enquiry.
> 
> **That **second sentence is where your second mark lives.

parts.problemMd:

|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Town centre | 3 | 4 |
| 2 | Inner suburb | 8 | 6 |
| 3 | Outer suburb | 19 | 8 |
| 4 | Rural fringe | 24 | 9 |
| 5 | Industrial area | 1 | 3 |

**Figure 1: **Solar panel count and environmental quality scores across five sites in Thornfield
parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
You have studied economic activity and energy as part of your own geographical enquiry.

**Evaluate** the reliability of the data you collected during your enquiry. In your answer, refer to both your **primary **and **secondary** **data**.

State the title of your geographical enquiry.
parts.solutionMd:
An investigation into types of energy use by people in Solus Street, Brightland, UK.

My primary data collection had both strengths and limitations in terms of reliability. **[K]** I used a structured questionnaire with closed questions to gather data from members of the public about their energy use. **[K]** This method produced quantitative data that was straightforward to compare and present as graphs. **[K]** However, the sample size was relatively small, which means the results may not represent the views of the whole community. **[U]** A larger sample would have improved reliability by reducing the risk of bias in the responses. **[U]**

The environmental quality survey (EQS) I completed at each site was also a primary method, but its reliability was limited by subjectivity. **[K]** Different students may score the same location differently depending on personal judgement, which reduces the consistency of the data.** [U]** To improve this, the group could have completed the EQS independently at each site and then compared scores, using an agreed scoring framework to reduce variation. **[Ap]**

My secondary data came from a government energy report on regional renewable energy trends. **[K]** This source was reliable because it was produced by an official body using large datasets. **[U]** However, the data was collected at a regional level, which made it difficult to apply directly to my local study area. **[Ap]**

Overall, my primary data was the less reliable of the two sources because of the small sample size and subjective scoring, though both sources together gave a more complete picture of energy use than either could alone. **[Ap]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**evaluate**' means the answer must make judgements about the reliability of the data, not simply describe what was collected. A strong answer will weigh up strengths and limitations and reach a supported conclusion.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a '**level of response**' approach. Each point made does not equal one mark.
> 
> A top-level 3 answer **[7 to 8 marks]** will:
> 
> - **AO1 ****[K]** demonstrate accurate knowledge of primary and secondary data collection methods used in an economic activity and energy enquiry
> - **AO2 ****[U]** show clear understanding of what makes data reliable or unreliable, including sample size, subjectivity, source credibility, and relevance
> - **AO3 ****[Ap]** apply evaluative judgement to their specific enquiry context, reaching a clear and supported conclusion about overall reliability
> 
> **No credit for:**
> 
> - Simply listing data collection methods without any evaluation of their reliability
> - A conclusion that only repeats earlier points without making a judgement
> - Responses that do not refer to both primary and secondary data as the question requires
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question and will depend on the fieldwork. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Visual surveys of energy infrastructure (wind turbines, solar panels, pylons)
> - Annotated photographs as qualitative primary data
> - Interviews with local stakeholders
> - Local council planning records as secondary data
> - News articles or energy company data as secondary sources
> 
> **Reliability:**
> 
> - Sample size and representativeness
> - Subjectivity of qualitative methods
> - Currency and relevance of secondary sources
> - Weather or time of day affecting primary data collection
> - Observer bias in visual surveys
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Describing the enquiry process rather than evaluating the reliability of the data
> - Focusing entirely on primary data and neglecting secondary data (or vice versa)
> - Using evaluative language in the introduction but drifting into description by the end
> - Writing a conclusion that does not make a clear judgement about overall reliability

parts.problemMd:
You have studied rural environments as part of your own geographical enquiry.

Evaluate the reliability of the data you collected during your enquiry. In your answer, refer to both your primary and secondary data.

State the title of your geographical enquiry.
parts.solutionMd:
The primary data I collected had both strengths and limitations when it came to reliability. **[Ap]**

I used a land-use survey at multiple sites, recording the dominant land use at each location on a structured recording sheet. **[K]**

This method was relatively reliable because it produced consistent, comparable data across all sites using the same criteria each time. **[Ap]**

However, some land uses were difficult to classify clearly, particularly where more than one type of farming was visible at the same site, which introduced an element of subjectivity into the results. **[U]** To improve reliability, the group could have used a more detailed classification system with clearer categories agreed in advance. **[Ap]**

I also completed a landscape quality survey at each site, which was a qualitative primary method. **[K]** This was less reliable than the land use survey because scores depended on individual judgement rather than measurable criteria. **[Ap]** Different members of the group may have scored the same site differently, reducing consistency across the dataset. **[U]**

My secondary data came from historic maps of the study area, which I used to compare past and present land use. **[K]** This source was reliable because it was produced by an official body and provided an objective record of land use at a specific point in time. **[U]** However, the maps were not always up-to-date for the most recent changes, which limited their usefulness for drawing conclusions about very recent farming changes. **[Ap]**

Overall, the secondary data was the more reliable of the two sources because it was produced systematically and was free from the observer bias that affected my primary surveys. **[Ap]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**evaluate**' means the answer must make judgements about the reliability of the data. It is not enough to describe what was collected. A strong answer will weigh up strengths and limitations across both primary and secondary data and reach a supported conclusion.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a '**level of response**' approach. Each point made does not equal one mark.
> 
> A top-level 3 answer **[7 to 8 marks]** will:
> 
> - **AO1 ****[K]** demonstrate accurate knowledge of primary and secondary data collection methods used in a rural environments enquiry
> - **AO2 ****[U]** show clear understanding of what makes data reliable or unreliable, including subjectivity, consistency, source credibility, and currency
> - **AO3 ****[Ap]** apply evaluative judgement to a specific enquiry context, reaching a clear and supported conclusion about overall reliability
> 
> **No credit for:**
> 
> - Simply listing data collection methods without any evaluation of their reliability
> - A conclusion that only repeats earlier points without making a judgement
> - Responses that do not refer to both primary and secondary data as the question requires
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question and will depend on the fieldwork. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Questionnaires with farmers or local residents as primary data
> - Annotated field sketches or photographs as qualitative primary data
> - Environmental quality surveys of the rural landscape
> - DEFRA agricultural census data as secondary data
> - Aerial photographs or satellite images from different time periods
> - Local planning authority records of land use change
> - Interviews with local stakeholders
> - Local council planning records as secondary data
> - News articles or energy company data as secondary sources
> 
> **Reliability:**
> 
> - Sample size and representativeness
> - Subjectivity of qualitative scoring methods
> - Currency and relevance of secondary sources
> - Weather or seasonal conditions affecting primary data collection
> - Difficulty of accessing remote rural sites consistently
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Describing the enquiry process rather than evaluating the reliability of the data
> - Focusing entirely on primary data and neglecting secondary data (or vice versa)
> - Using evaluative language in the introduction but drifting into description by the end
> - Writing a conclusion that does not make a clear comparative judgement between primary and secondary data

parts.problemMd:
Using **Figure 1**, describe the relationship between the environmental quality score and the percentage of buildings in poor repair.

| Site | Location | EQS score (out of 20) | Percentage of buildings in poor repair (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Town centre (CBD) | 7 | 38 |
| 2 | Inner city | 9 | 29 |
| 3 | Inner suburb | 13 | 14 |
| 4 | Outer suburb | 17 | 6 |
| 5 | Rural fringe | 19 | 2 |

**Figure 1:** Environmental quality scores and building condition across five sites in Millbrook
parts.solutionMd:
Figure 1 shows a clear negative correlation between the two variables: as the environmental quality score increases, the percentage of buildings in poor repair decreases. **[1]** For example, the town centre (Site 1) has the lowest EQS score of 7 and the highest percentage of buildings in poor repair at 38%, while the rural fringe (Site 5) has the highest EQS score of 19 and only 2% of buildings in poor repair. **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**describe**' means the answer should state what the data shows. No explanation of why the relationship exists is required.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for correctly identifying the overall relationship (negative correlation: as EQS score increases, percentage of buildings in poor repair decreases)
> - **One mark** for supporting this with specific data from Figure 1
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Attempting to explain why the relationship exists rather than describing what it shows
> - Describing only one site rather than the overall pattern across all five sites
> - Stating there is no relationship when a clear negative correlation is visible in the data

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Name **the type of relationship first (positive, negative, or no correlation), then back it up immediately with data from the table.
> 
> **Always **quote both variables together, for example EQS score and building condition, rather than describing each column separately. That paired approach is what earns the second mark.

Using** Figure 1**, explain** one advantage **and **one disadvantage** of presenting the environmental quality score data as a line graph.
parts.solutionMd:
One advantage of a line graph is that it clearly shows the trend in environmental quality scores as distance from the town centre increases. **[1]** For example, the steady rise from a score of 7 at Site 1 to 19 at Site 5 would appear as a clear upward line, making the spatial pattern across Millbrook immediately visible to the reader. **[1]**

However, one disadvantage is that a line graph implies continuous change between the five sites, suggesting that environmental quality increases smoothly and evenly across the town. **[1]** In reality, the data was only collected at five specific points, so the line between those points is an assumption rather than a measured fact, which could be misleading. **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**explain**' means each advantage and disadvantage must be developed with a reason rather than simply stated.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for a valid advantage of a line graph
> - **One mark** for development of that advantage with reference to Figure 1
> - **One mark** for a valid disadvantage of a line graph
> - **One mark **for development of that disadvantage
> 
> **[4 marks]**
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> **Advantages:**
> 
> - Clearly shows trends and patterns across the transect
> - Allows the reader to see the direction and rate of change between sites
> - Effective for showing data collected at points along a continuous transect
> - Easy to read and interpret at a glance
> 
> **Disadvantages **
> 
> - Implies continuous change between data points that were not actually measured
> - Cannot show two variables (EQS score and building condition) on the same axis without a dual axis, which can be confusing

> - Discussing a different graph type rather than focusing on line graphs, as the question requires
> - Writing that a line graph 'looks good' or 'is easy to draw' without any geographical justification

parts.problemMd:
You have studied urban environments as part of your own geographical enquiry.

Evaluate the reliability of the data you collected during your enquiry. In your answer, refer to both your primary and secondary data.

State the title of your geographical enquiry.
parts.solutionMd:
The primary data I collected provided a useful starting point for my enquiry, but its reliability had clear limitations. **[U]**

I used an environmental quality survey (EQS) to score each site along my transect out of 20 across a range of criteria, including air quality, noise levels, and the condition of buildings. **[K]** This method produced quantitative data that was straightforward to compare between sites and to present as a line graph. **[U]**

However, the EQS relied heavily on personal judgement, particularly for criteria such as air quality, which is difficult to assess accurately by observation alone. **[Ap]** This subjectivity reduced the reliability of the data because different students in the group may have scored the same site differently, making direct comparisons between sites less consistent. **[U]**

I also used a building condition survey as a second primary method, recording the percentage of buildings in a poor state of repair at each site.** [K]** This was more reliable than the EQS because it used a clearer, more objective criterion that was easier to apply consistently across all sites. **[Ap]**

My secondary data came from the local council's environmental quality report for the study area.** [K] **This was a reliable source because it was produced using systematic data collection methods across the whole town rather than at just five points. **[Ap]** However, the report was two years old at the time of my enquiry, which meant it may not have reflected the most recent changes to environmental quality in the area. **[Ap]**

On balance, the secondary data was more reliable than my primary EQS data because it was based on a larger sample and used objective measurement criteria rather than personal judgement. **[Ap]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The command word '**evaluate**' means the answer must make judgements about the reliability of the data, not simply describe what was collected. A strong answer will weigh up strengths and limitations and reach a supported conclusion.
> 
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a '**level of response**' approach. Each point made does not equal one mark.
> 
> A top-level 3 answer **[7 to 8 marks]** will:
> 
> - **AO1 ****[K]** demonstrate accurate knowledge of primary and secondary data collection methods used in an urban environments enquiry
> - **AO2 ****[U]** show clear understanding of what makes data reliable or unreliable, including sample size, subjectivity, source credibility, and relevance
> - **AO3 ****[Ap]** apply evaluative judgement to their specific enquiry context, reaching a clear and supported conclusion about overall reliability
> 
> **No credit for:**
> 
> - Simply listing data collection methods without any evaluation of their reliability
> - A conclusion that only repeats earlier points without making a judgement
> - Responses that do not refer to both primary and secondary data as the question requires
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question and will depend on the fieldwork. Alternative information that could be provided in the answer includes:
> 
> - Structured questionnaires with members of the public as primary data
> - Annotated photographs or field sketches as qualitative primary data
> - Land use surveys along the transect
> - Census data on housing conditions or deprivation as secondary data
> - Local authority regeneration reports or planning documents
> - Historic maps or aerial photographs showing urban change over time
> 
> **Reliability:**
> 
> - Subjectivity of EQS scoring criteria
> - Sample size and representativeness of the transect
> - Observer bias in visual surveys
> - Time of day or weather conditions affecting primary data collection
> - Consistency of data collection between different group members
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Describing the fieldwork process rather than evaluating the reliability of the data collected
> - Focusing entirely on one type of data and neglecting the other
> - Using evaluative language only in the conclusion rather than spreading judgements throughout
> - Writing a conclusion that does not make a clear comparative judgement between primary and secondary data

> **[exam-tip]**
> **Be specific** about your methods. 'I collected data' earns no marks. 'I used an EQS scored out of 20 across six criteria' earns marks because it shows precise knowledge of your own enquiry.
